title: Statistical inference and resource allocation in expert data production
markdown:
## 1 How selective review changes quality measurement In production RLHF pipelines, the policy for routing submissions to review changes the statistical properties of the observed sample. Let $`X`$ denote observable task features, including the domain, prompt complexity, and contributor history, and let $`Y \in \{0, 1\}`$ indicate whether the original submission contains an error under fixed acceptance criteria. The true conditional error probability is $`q(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid X = x)`$. Let $`S = 1`$ indicate selection for an independent reference audit. Conditional on $`X`$, selection is randomized with probability $`\pi(x) > 0`$ and is independent of the reference label, which has not yet been observed. An operational dashboard that uses the error fraction among verified submissions to estimate population quality targets: $$ E[Y \mid S = 1] = \frac{E[\pi(X)q(X)]}{E[\pi(X)]} $$ $$ E[Y \mid S = 1] - E[Y] = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\pi(X), q(X))}{E[\pi(X)]} $$ When review successfully targets higher true error risk, the covariance between audit probability $`\pi(X)`$ and true defect probability $`q(X)`$ is strictly positive. A higher error detection rate in the reviewed sample can therefore reflect more effective risk targeting; it does not by itself establish that production quality has deteriorated. These identities describe the distribution of a selected item. In a finite batch, the observed error fraction also has a random denominator, so it must be distinguished from the population expression above. The same selection mechanism affects expert rankings. Let $`a_{jh}`$ be the probability that expert $`j`$ answers a task in stratum $`h`$ correctly, and let $`p_{jht}`$ describe that expert's assigned task mix in period $`t`$. Observed accuracy changes with the task mix even if underlying ability remains constant: $$ A_{jt} = \sum_h p_{jht} a_{jh}, \qquad A_{j,t+1} - A_{jt} = \sum_h (p_{jh,t+1} - p_{jht}) a_{jh} $$ Comparisons across periods therefore require a fixed target task mix $`w_h`$ and standardized accuracy: $$ A_j^{\text{std}} = \sum_h w_h a_{jh} $$ Overlapping assignments or shared anchor cases support estimation within each stratum. In the project's production routing engine, I used a conjugate Beta-Binomial model for each contributor's reliability within a task stratum. Given a prior $`\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_{0h}, \beta_{0h})`$ and $`n_{jht}`$ audited tasks with $`k_{jht}`$ verified successes, the posterior $`\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_{0h} + k_{jht}, \beta_{0h} + n_{jht} - k_{jht})`$ provides shrinkage-regularized point estimates and credible intervals that account for unequal sample sizes across comparable audits. Pooling tasks of different difficulty, rubric versions, and selection mechanisms into a single unstratified binomial sample leaves the selection bias unresolved. These statistical requirements also guide the choice of reviewer models and allocation methods. [Dawid-Skene](https://doi.org/10.2307/2346806) models describe differences in reviewer confusion matrices relative to latent ground truth. [DeCCaF](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.06906v1) incorporates task conditions, error costs, and reviewer capacity into human-AI deferral, including the effect of difficult assignments on naive evaluations of expert performance. The production architecture connects selective review assignment with unbiased population quality inference in ongoing post-training work ([Dawid-Skene](https://doi.org/10.2307/2346806); [DeCCaF](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.06906v1)). ## 2 Correcting predictions with audits to estimate population quality Fix a production batch of $`N`$ original submissions, its acceptance criteria, and its latent reference labels $`Y_1, \dots, Y_N`$. The inferential target is the finite-batch error rate $`\mu = N^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i`$. Let $`f_i \in [0, 1]`$ be a fixed, inexpensive risk prediction combining contributor reliability posteriors, task complexity, and automated heuristic checks. Assign audit probability $`\pi_i \in [\pi_{\min}, 1]`$ and draw $`S_i \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)`$ independently across submissions. Predictions and sampling probabilities are locked before the current batch's reference labels are revealed. We used a prediction-assisted estimator with inverse-probability-weighted (IPW) residual correction: $$ \hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ f_i + \frac{S_i}{\pi_i} (Y_i - f_i) \right] $$ Its design-based validity follows from the conditional expectation below. Write the prediction residual as $`e_i = Y_i - f_i`$ and condition on the fixed batch, predictions, and sampling probabilities: $$ \hat{\mu} - \mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left( \frac{S_i}{\pi_i} - 1 \right) e_i, \qquad E_S[\hat{\mu} - \mu] = 0 $$ Inverse-probability weighting restores the population representation altered by selective verification. Predictions reduce the residual variation that human expert audits must resolve. Design-based unbiasedness does not require $`f_i = q(X_i)`$: inaccurate predictions may reduce efficiency, but the estimator remains unbiased under the specified Bernoulli sampling design. The estimator follows established active statistical inference principles ([Active Statistical Inference: mean estimation and sampling design](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.03208v3)). For production use, I defined procedures for freezing the audited objects, recording rubric version histories, and retaining the telemetry needed for optimization. Original and revised submissions must be retained as separate database entities. Estimating $`\hat{\mu}_{\text{raw}}`$ on frozen originals and $`\hat{\mu}_{\text{final}}`$ on post-review deliverables distinguishes defects introduced during initial production from those corrected through review. When post-training criteria change, a shared set of anchor cases is adjudicated under both rubric versions. Submissions from different periods can then be compared under a common reference version, preventing stricter acceptance standards from being misread as declining contributor ability. ## 3 Allocating audit effort by residual uncertainty and cost Independent Bernoulli sampling removes cross-item covariance terms and gives the exact design variance: $$ \operatorname{Var}_S(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1 - \pi_i}{\pi_i} e_i^2 $$ This expression defines the audit allocation objective: audit effort should address uncertainty left unresolved by automated risk predictions. For a binary error label with conditional error probability $`q_i`$, the expected squared residual has two components: $$ m_i := E[(Y_i - f_i)^2 \mid X_i] = q_i(1 - q_i) + (q_i - f_i)^2 $$ The terms are the conditional Bernoulli variance $`q_i(1 - q_i)`$ and the squared calibration error $`(q_i - f_i)^2`$. A high error probability $`q_i`$ need not imply high inferential value. If a task category is almost certain to contain an error ($`q_i \approx 1`$) and the predictor recognizes this ($`f_i \approx 1`$), then $`m_i \approx 0`$. An independent reference audit of that item contributes less information about population quality than an audit of a moderately risky item whose outcome remains uncertain ($`q_i \approx 0.5`$). A remediation model measures the benefit of correcting high-risk tasks; a measurement model evaluates how audits improve population estimates. Let $`c_i > 0`$ be the empirical cost of an independent reference audit, calibrated by reconciling platform review logs with Hubstaff active-work telemetry, and let $`B`$ be the expected audit-cost budget. When the true residual second moments $`m_i > 0`$ are known, the optimal design solves: $$ \min_{\pi} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{m_i}{\pi_i} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^N c_i \pi_i \le B, \quad \pi_{\min} \le \pi_i \le 1 $$ The omitted constant $`-\sum_i m_i`$ in the variance numerator does not depend on the allocation $`\pi`$. For probabilities strictly between their bounds, the Lagrangian first-order condition gives the clipped square-root allocation: $$ -\frac{m_i}{\pi_i^2} + \lambda c_i = 0 \implies \pi_i^* = \operatorname{clip}_{[\pi_{\min}, 1]} \left( \sqrt{\frac{m_i}{\lambda c_i}} \right) $$ For a budget below the cost of a full audit, $`\lambda > 0`$ is chosen to satisfy the budget constraint. The multiplier need not be unique when clipping is active, and feasibility requires $`B \ge \pi_{\min} \sum_i c_i`$. If the budget covers a full audit, every item is audited ($`\pi_i^* = 1`$). The square-root rule assigns higher sampling intensity to larger expected residuals and lower intensity to more expensive audits. A positive probability floor $`\pi_{\min}`$ maintains coverage across the task space and bounds IPW weights. Production allocation uses regularized stratum estimates $`\hat{m}_i > 0`$ from earlier independent audits or a pilot calibration batch. The true $`m_i`$ defines the optimality analysis; the estimates $`\hat{m}_i`$ determine operational allocation. Residuals are estimated at the level of `(task stratum × criteria version × cost stratum)` to avoid fitting unstable parameters to individual submissions. The budget $`B`$ constrains expected audit cost per batch. A workflow requiring an exact integer audit count needs a feasible fixed-size sampling design whose first-order inclusion probabilities sum to that count. Its variance depends on joint inclusion probabilities, and its inclusion probabilities need not equal the Bernoulli optimum $`\pi_i^*`$. ## 4 Allocation gains and the conditions they require Using the same predictor, the efficiency gain from allocation based on residuals and costs can be derived relative to uniform sampling. The derivation also identifies when the gain vanishes or the allocation fails. Let $`C = \sum_{i=1}^N c_i`$, so the uniform sampling probability at the same expected cost is $`p = B / C`$. If the true residual second moments $`m_i`$ are available and no optimal probability reaches a clipping boundary, averaging design variance over the conditional label distribution gives: $$ V_{\text{uniform}} = \frac{1}{N^2} \left[ \frac{C \sum_i m_i}{B} - \sum_i m_i \right] $$ $$ V_{\text{optimal}} = \frac{1}{N^2} \left[ \frac{\left(\sum_i \sqrt{m_i c_i}\right)^2}{B} - \sum_i m_i \right] $$ If all items within a fixed task stratum share a sampling probability, substituting that stratum's finite-batch mean squared residual for $`m_i`$ makes these expressions exact finite-batch identities. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives: $$ V_{\text{uniform}} - V_{\text{optimal}} = \frac{C \sum_i m_i - \left(\sum_i \sqrt{m_i c_i}\right)^2}{N^2 B} \ge 0 $$ Equality holds if and only if $`m_i / c_i`$ is constant across items. Efficiency gains depend on identifiable variation in residual second moment per unit audit cost. With homogeneous residuals and costs, the optimal allocation is uniform. If clipping is active at $`\pi_{\min}`$ or $`1`$, constrained optimization remains no worse than a feasible uniform policy; the gain can be evaluated directly from the clipped primal objective. The analysis also quantifies the variance penalty from model misspecification. If allocation uses inaccurate residual estimates $`\hat{m}_i`$ and neither allocation is clipped, the excess variance relative to the true optimum is: $$ V(\hat{\pi}) - V(\pi^*) = \frac{1}{N^2 B} \left[ \left( \sum_i \sqrt{\hat{m}_i c_i} \right) \left( \sum_i \frac{m_i \sqrt{c_i}}{\sqrt{\hat{m}_i}} \right) - \left( \sum_i \sqrt{m_i c_i} \right)^2 \right] \ge 0 $$ Severely underestimating $`\hat{m}_i`$ in any part of the task space increases the penalty through the denominator $`\sqrt{\hat{m}_i}`$. A positive sampling floor $`\pi_{\min}`$ limits the worst-case variance increase. Active and uniform sampling probabilities can also be combined without changing the budget: $$ \pi_i(\rho) = (1 - \rho)\hat{\pi}_i + \rho p $$ The shrinkage weight $`\rho \in [0, 1]`$ can be tuned using independent calibration batches ([Robust Sampling for Active Statistical Inference](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08991v1)). ## 5 Allocating review by expected loss reduction Statistical auditing measures population quality with minimum variance. Operational review removes defects from the current batch before it is delivered for training. The two objectives are estimation precision and delivered quality. For task $`i`$ under handling action $`a`$, such as direct acceptance, peer review, expert adjudication, or contributor revision, let $`r_{ia}`$ be the expected error loss remaining after the action, $`d_{ia}`$ its operational cost, and $`t_{iaj}`$ the time required from specialist $`j`$, measured through platform and Hubstaff telemetry. Binary assignment decisions $`z_{ia} \in \{0, 1\}`$ solve: $$ \min_{z} F(z) = \sum_{i,a} z_{ia}(r_{ia} + \eta d_{ia}) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_a z_{ia} = 1, \quad \sum_{i,a} z_{ia} t_{iaj} \le H_j \quad \forall j $$ Here $`H_j`$ is the specialist's available time, and $`\eta \ge 0`$ converts resource cost to the scale of error loss ([DeCCaF: capacity constraints and global assignment](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.06906v1)). When review costs are equal and each reviewed task uses one slot, the optimal priority order is determined by marginal remediation gain $`\Delta_i = r_{i0} - r_{i1}`$. Initial risk $`r_{i0}`$ measures the risk before review. Missing external evidence may leave a high-risk task difficult to repair through one additional review, giving a small $`\Delta_i`$. A self-contained calculation error in a moderate-risk task may be fully correctable, giving a large $`\Delta_k`$. Moving one review slot from task $`i`$ to task $`k`$ changes total expected loss by: $$ \Delta F = (r_{i0} + r_{k1}) - (r_{i1} + r_{k0}) = \Delta_i - \Delta_k $$ Whenever $`\Delta_k > \Delta_i`$, the exchange strictly reduces delivered defect loss, regardless of the initial risk ordering. Error in the action-risk estimates also determines a performance bound for review allocation. Suppose $`|\hat{r}_{ia} - r_{ia}| \le \delta`$ for every feasible action, costs and capacities are known, and $`\hat{z}`$ minimizes the predicted objective $`\hat{F}(z)`$. Relative to the true optimal feasible assignment $`z^*`$: $$ F(\hat{z}) \le \hat{F}(\hat{z}) + N\delta \le \hat{F}(z^*) + N\delta \le F(z^*) + 2N\delta $$ The bound identifies post-action residual loss $`r_{ia}`$ as the empirical quantity that must be calibrated, providing a basis for randomized pilot trials across permitted review actions. The remediation and measurement budgets can be combined in a batch-level mixed-integer convex program (MICP). Let $`\tau^2`$ be the target variance ceiling for the quality estimate, $`B_{\text{total}}`$ the total cost budget, and $`V_{\hat{m}}(\pi) = N^{-2}\sum_i (1 - \pi_i)\hat{m}_i / \pi_i`$ the planning variance under the calibrated residual model: $$ \min_{z, \pi} \sum_{i,a} z_{ia}\hat{r}_{ia} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i,a} z_{ia} d_{ia} + \sum_i c_i \pi_i \le B_{\text{total}}, \quad V_{\hat{m}}(\pi) \le \tau^2 $$ $$ \sum_a z_{ia} = 1, \quad z_{ia} \in \{0, 1\}, \quad \sum_{i,a} z_{ia} t_{iaj} \le H_j^{\text{review}} \ \forall j, \quad \pi_{\min} \le \pi_i \le 1 $$ The hard capacity $`H_j^{\text{review}}`$ is allocated to remediation actions. Reference audits are scheduled independently on frozen original submissions. The precision ceiling is model-based and requires independent audits to check residual calibration. An expected audit-cost constraint does not impose a hard limit on realized audit hours. An infeasible program indicates a conflict among the precision target, feasible review assignments, and available engineering budget. ## 6 Reproducible experiments at equal cost The following synthetic experiments test these mathematical mechanisms using publicly specified parameters. Their results describe algorithm behavior under those parameters; proprietary client telemetry is outside the disclosure scope. A fixed batch contains $`N = 10,000`$ submissions in three strata of $`6,000`$, $`3,000`$, and $`1,000`$ items, with $`60`$, $`300`$, and $`350`$ errors, respectively. The true batch defect rate is $`\mu = 7.10\%`$. Unit audit costs are $`1`$, $`1.5`$, and $`3`$ across the three strata. Every policy has an expected audit budget of $`B = 2,000`$ units and a minimum sampling probability of $`\pi_{\min} = 3\%`$. Risk predictions for the three strata are $`2\%`$, $`8\%`$, and $`30\%`$. The batch average is $`6.60\%`$, which differs from the true defect rate by $`0.50`$ percentage points. The cost-aware allocation uses the true within-stratum mean squared residuals, representing ideal calibration. The misspecified policy reverses the residual ordering across strata. With predictions, budget, and submissions held fixed, $`200,000`$ independent Monte Carlo repetitions verify the analytical variance formulas:

Under ideal residual calibration, the standard deviation of the population quality estimate falls by **9.33%**, a **17.79%** reduction in variance. Under the high-risk-first policy, the uncorrected error detection rate averages **19.60%**, overstating the population defect rate. IPW residual correction recovers **7.1015%**. The policy oversamples the more expensive third stratum, increasing estimation variance by **33.77%**. Across all five policies, Monte Carlo variances differ from the analytical formulas by no more than $`0.5\%`$. A separate exact allocation experiment isolates the effect of remediation. Two task groups contain $`100`$ items each, with initial error risks of $`0.40`$ and $`0.15`$. Additional review reduces these risks to $`0.30`$ ($`\Delta_1 = 0.10`$) and $`0.01`$ ($`\Delta_2 = 0.14`$), respectively. Review costs are equal, and capacity is $`100`$ items. Ranking by initial risk leaves $`100(0.30) + 100(0.15) = 45`$ expected errors. Ranking by expected loss reduction ($`\Delta_i`$) leaves $`100(0.40) + 100(0.01) = 41`$ expected errors, reducing expected defect loss by **8.89%** at the same review volume. ## 7 Production validation and evaluation criteria I defined separate production evaluations for statistical quality inference and operational defect control. Errors detected in a targeted queue indicate how well review locates defects. Improvements in delivered quality must be assessed through the defects that remain and the associated costs. 1. **Inference on frozen, adjudicated batches.** Compare uniform sampling, legacy high-risk routing, cost-aware residual allocation, and defensive mixtures against complete independent adjudication. Assess bias, mean squared error (MSE), and interval coverage within task strata and rubric versions. 2. **Remediation trials at matched capacity.** Compare legacy tiered rules with marginal-gain ($`\Delta_i`$) action allocation at equal total specialist hours. Measure severe defects remaining in the final post-training corpus and the fully loaded cost per accepted submission. Beginning in September 2023, I led the development of contributor reliability records, tiered review workflows, and random reference audits, establishing the project's operating standards for expert collaboration, quality measurement, and resource allocation. The analysis specifies the sampling, calibration, and capacity assumptions under which quality estimation is unbiased and audit allocation is optimal when residual second moments are correctly specified. The synthetic benchmarks test these mechanisms under their stated conditions.
